examples.Institutional: Labels that frame any artist pushback as "ego," "entitlement" or "not being a team player," so negotiation is recorded as a personality problem rather than a business issue.
examples.Civilizational: "Gratitude means silence" — the industry script that turns any objection into a moral failing and makes compliance look like good character.

tactics.name: Financial Control
tactics.definition: Restricting access to resources to enforce compliance.
tactics.also_called: Economic Abuse; Economic Coercion; Financial Isolation

examples.Individual: "I'll hold your advance and pay your rent from it — you're not good with money" — your manager now controls the account and you have to ask for cash to buy groceries.
examples.Institutional: Deal structures where advances, tour support and per diems flow through the label or management, and recoupment keeps the artist's royalties at zero while the obligations continue.
examples.Civilizational: "Money problems mean you're bad at business" — the cultural story that blames artists for being broke and hides how financial dependence was built into the deal.

tactics.name: Sexual Coercion
tactics.definition: Using power to override consent.

examples.Individual: A powerful producer suggests the "real session" happens back at his place and makes clear the record depends on it — career power used to override your consent, and something to take to a support service, not to handle alone.
examples.Institutional: Companies that respond to reports of sexual misconduct by quietly moving the artist off the project, settling with NDAs and keeping the powerful person working — the system protecting itself.
examples.Civilizational: The long-told story that "that's just how the business works" for anyone who wants to make it — a myth that hides coercion and makes those harmed feel it was the price of entry.

tactics.name: Reproductive Coercion
tactics.definition: Controlling reproductive choices through institutional pressure.

examples.Individual: "A pregnancy right now would kill the album cycle — you need to think about what you really want" — the manager says it as career advice, but your reproductive choice is now tied to your deal.
examples.Institutional: Contracts and tour schedules with no room for pregnancy or parenting, where artists who start families lose marketing support, tour slots or their place on the roster.
examples.Civilizational: The industry belief that a woman's career window is short and must come before family — a timing expectation that pressures reproductive choices without anyone saying it outright.

tactics.name: Extinction Bursts
tactics.definition: Dramatic escalation when control methods stop working.

examples.Individual: When you tell your manager you won't renew, the calls start — late-night voice notes, messages to your bandmates, threats about your masters — the pressure spiking the moment the usual hold stops working.
examples.Institutional: Labels that respond to an artist's exit notice with a sudden wave of default letters, release freezes and public statements, escalating hard once quieter forms of control fail.
examples.Civilizational: The industry story that a messy, explosive split is just "drama" — which hides how escalation often signals that someone has lost control and is trying to get it back.

tactics.name: Negative Reinforcement Traps
tactics.definition: Applying pressure until compliance, then removing it — training that compliance equals relief.

examples.Individual: The label holds back your release and ignores your calls until you agree to the extra brand deal — then suddenly the emails warm up, the release is back on and everyone is friendly again.
examples.Institutional: Business affairs teams that keep payments, approvals and releases stuck until an artist accepts new terms, and then release everything at once — teaching that giving in is the only way to make the pressure stop.
examples.Civilizational: The industry story that "things got easier once I stopped fighting" — which recasts relief from pressure as wisdom rather than conditioning.

tactics.name: Phobia Indoctrination / Catastrophizing
tactics.definition: Exaggerating consequences to extract compliance.

examples.Individual: "If you leave this label, you'll never work again — no one will touch you and your fans will forget you in a month" — the manager paints the worst ending to keep you in place.
examples.Institutional: Contract renegotiations framed as all-or-nothing, where any change is presented as a risk to the entire release, the tour and the artist's future.
examples.Civilizational: The shared fear that one wrong move ends a career forever — so exaggerated predictions sound like realism and keep people from making changes.

tactics.name: Strategic Chaos / Crisis Manufacturing
tactics.definition: Constant emergencies preventing strategic thinking.

examples.Individual: Every week there's a new emergency — the venue fell through, the label is furious, the single needs re-recording by tomorrow — and you never get a calm moment to ask about your contract.
examples.Institutional: Management firms and tour operations where constant last-minute crises are the norm, so artists and crew stay reactive and never step back to see the pattern.
examples.Civilizational: The romantic picture of the industry as permanent chaos — which makes running from fire to fire look normal and leaves no space for planning or questioning.

tactics.name: Time Control
tactics.definition: Dictating how every hour is spent to prevent autonomous thought.

examples.Individual: "Your day starts at six with vocal warmups, then content, then the studio, then the gym — no free time until the album's done" — the manager's schedule leaves no hour that is yours.
examples.Institutional: Content calendars, release plans and promo schedules that plan every day of an artist's life months ahead, leaving no room for rest, reflection or independent decisions.
examples.Civilizational: The cultural message that "the grind never stops" — which treats total control of an artist's time as dedication and makes free time feel like slacking.

tactics.name: Sleep Deprivation
tactics.definition: Disrupting rest to reduce cognitive and emotional resistance.

examples.Individual: After the show you're kept up for the after-party, then an early flight, then a radio interview — and when you say you're exhausted, the tour manager says "sleep is for after the tour."
examples.Institutional: Touring schedules built around overnight drives, back-to-back shows and dawn promo, where sleep is treated as optional and the people most tired are least able to question anything.
examples.Civilizational: The industry badge of pride in sleepless tours and all-night sessions — which makes exhaustion look like commitment and hides how it wears down judgment.

tactics.name: Narrative Monopoly
tactics.definition: Controlling the dominant story so alternative accounts can't gain traction.

examples.Individual: After you leave the band, the lead singer gives interviews about how you "walked out on everyone" — and the story repeats everywhere before you've said a word.
examples.Institutional: Labels and publicists that control press releases, fan messaging and industry gossip after a split, so only their account of what happened gets airtime.
examples.Civilizational: The belief that the version from the bigger name is the true one — so the official story becomes history and other accounts sound like sour grapes.

tactics.name: Mobility Control
tactics.definition: Restricting physical movement to enforce submission.

examples.Individual: "You can't go home for your sister's wedding — we've got a show that night" — the manager holds your passport "for safekeeping" on the international leg.
examples.Institutional: Tour contracts and handler arrangements that restrict where artists and crew can go, require permission to leave the hotel and control travel documents — movement managed as policy.
examples.Civilizational: The belief that touring artists belong on the road and travel is part of the deal — which makes restricting someone's freedom of movement look like logistics.

tactics.name: Body Autonomy Violations
tactics.definition: Controlling the physical body under institutional justification.

examples.Individual: "Lose the weight before the video shoot or we'll find someone who will" — the stylist and the A&R decide what your body must look like for the release.
examples.Institutional: Image clauses, styling approvals and wellness plans that give the label control over a performer's appearance, diet and physical changes "for the brand."
examples.Civilizational: The industry belief that an artist's body is part of the product — which makes controlling weight, looks and health feel like marketing instead of a violation.

tactics.name: Role Assignment
tactics.definition: Assigning fixed identities that dictate expectation and treatment.
tactics.also_called: Identification as Identity Assignment; Identity Narrowing; Role Confinement

examples.Individual: "You're the quiet one, you don't do interviews, you just play bass" — your bandmates and manager fix you in a role and push back every time you step out of it.
examples.Institutional: Labels that assign artists a persona — the bad girl, the boy next door, the sad songwriter — and penalize any change in style or public behavior that doesn't fit the brief.
examples.Civilizational: The cultural habit of seeing artists as types rather than people — which locks performers into roles the market expects and makes growth look like betrayal.

tactics.name: Forced Dependency
tactics.definition: Eliminating the ability to function outside the system.
tactics.also_called: Dependency Engineering; Dependency Installation; Device Dependency; Ecosystem Embedding

examples.Individual: Your manager handles your money, your lawyer, your housing and your travel — and when you think about leaving, you realize you don't even know how to book your own flight.
examples.Institutional: Multi-rights deals and all-in management setups that route every service through the company, so the artist cannot record, tour, sell merch or get paid without them.
examples.Civilizational: "We'll take care of the business side, just focus on the music" — the industry promise that leaves artists unable to function outside the system that holds them.

tactics.name: Silence as Policy
tactics.definition: Making certain topics undiscussable through emotional consequence.
tactics.also_called: Challenge Suppression; Organizational Silence Engineering; Permanent Silencing

examples.Individual: You mention the producer's behavior to your manager, and he looks away and says "let's not go there, it'll only cause problems for you" — the subject closes for good.
examples.Institutional: Labels and touring companies where raising harassment, money questions or mental health draws cold responses, so staff and artists learn which topics are off-limits.
examples.Civilizational: The unspoken code that "what happens on the road stays on the road" — which keeps whole categories of harm out of conversation by making them socially costly to name.

tactics.name: Children as Leverage
tactics.definition: Using children's wellbeing as a tool of control over adults.

examples.Individual: "Your daughter's career depends on you signing this tonight" — the production company presses the parent of a child performer, using the child's future as leverage. Worries about a child's welfare belong with child-protection services or a trusted professional.
examples.Institutional: Development programs and child-performer contracts that tie a parent's income, access or standing to the child staying in the deal — the child's wellbeing used as a lever on the adult.
examples.Civilizational: The belief that a talented child's chance must be grabbed at any cost — which makes pressuring families through their children look like supporting a dream.

tactics.name: Micromanagement
tactics.definition: Controlling minute details to erode autonomous function.
tactics.also_called: Algorithmic Management; Autonomy Displacement; Pattern Recognition as Evaluation; Teacher Displacement

examples.Individual: The producer redoes every take you record, rewrites your melodies, adjusts your mic position and questions every breath — until you stop trusting your own ear.
examples.Institutional: Labels that require approval for every post, outfit, lyric and interview answer, so artists can't make any decision without sign-off.
examples.Civilizational: The belief that a successful release needs total control from above — which turns oversight of every detail into "quality control" and erodes the artist's confidence.

tactics.name: Performance Monitoring
tactics.definition: Constant evaluation that installs hypervigilance.

examples.Individual: Your manager sends you your streaming numbers every morning with a comment on whether you're "trending up or down" — and you start checking them every hour.
examples.Institutional: Labels and platforms that rate artists on daily metrics, engagement targets and playlist performance, holding reviews that keep everyone scanning for the next judgment.
examples.Civilizational: The cultural shift that turns every artist into a dashboard — making constant scrutiny feel like progress and keeping performers anxious instead of creative.

tactics.name: Controlled Communication
tactics.definition: Dictating how, when, and whether you may speak.
tactics.also_called: Communication Chain Restriction; Constraining Verbal Expression; Vocal Regulation

examples.Individual: "Don't post anything about the tour until I approve it, and run your interview answers by me first" — the manager now decides when and how you speak in public.
examples.Institutional: Labels that script press statements, ban artists from talking to journalists without a publicist and control every public word under "media training."
examples.Civilizational: The belief that an artist's voice belongs to the brand — so having your speech managed feels like protection instead of silencing.

tactics.name: Rage as Regulation
tactics.definition: Using anger or its threat to control the environment.

examples.Individual: The label head explodes when the single underperforms, slamming the desk and shouting until the room goes silent — everyone leaves careful never to set him off again.
examples.Institutional: Studios and management offices where outbursts from senior figures are tolerated as "passion," so the people around them adjust their behavior to avoid the next eruption.
examples.Civilizational: The romantic idea of the tortured genius whose temper comes with the talent — which excuses rage and makes everyone else responsible for managing it.

tactics.name: Fear Installation
tactics.definition: Creating persistent dread through unpredictable consequences.

examples.Individual: One week your manager praises you, the next he says the label might drop you, and you never know which version you'll get — so you live waiting for the next blow.
examples.Institutional: Labels with unclear criteria for dropping artists, where roster cuts happen without warning and the remaining artists stay anxious about who will be next.
examples.Civilizational: The common feeling that any career can disappear overnight — which makes constant fear normal and makes people grateful for anything that feels stable.

tactics.name: Managed Perception
tactics.definition: Controlling how the system appears to outsiders.

examples.Individual: After the tour you were burned out on, the label posts a video of you smiling backstage with the caption "best family ever" — and fans believe it.
examples.Institutional: Companies that publish glossy behind-the-scenes content, wellness statements and happy artist testimonials, so the public sees a caring industry while the real conditions stay hidden.
examples.Civilizational: The glamour image of the music business — which makes it hard for outsiders to believe stories about exploitation and easy to dismiss those who speak up.

tactics.name: Omnipresence / Demonstrating Omnipotence
tactics.definition: The sense that the system is always watching, always present, always ahead of you.

examples.Individual: "Nice dinner at the place downtown last night" — your manager mentions it casually, though you never told him where you went.
examples.Institutional: A tight network of labels, agents and promoters who all talk to each other, so an artist who leaves one company feels the presence of that company in every room.
examples.Civilizational: The belief that the industry knows everything and forgets nothing — which keeps artists cautious long after they've left and makes freedom feel temporary.

tactics.name: Punishment by Proxy
tactics.definition: After a conflict between two people, trouble arrives for a third person the target cares about.

examples.Individual: After you argue with the label head over your contract, your younger brother suddenly loses his spot as your tour photographer — the conflict was yours, but the cost lands on someone you love.
examples.Institutional: When an artist challenges the management company, the session players and crew who work with that artist find their other bookings drying up — pressure routed through the people around them.
examples.Civilizational: Everyone knows that falling out with the wrong person can cost your friends their work, so artists weigh every fight by who else might pay for it.

tactics.name: Emotional Blackmail
tactics.definition: A request is tied to the relationship: do this, or the closeness, approval or safety you rely on will be withdrawn.
tactics.also_called: Conditional Safety; Emotional Blackmail via Implicit Consequence; Revocation Threat

examples.Individual: "I've fought for you with the label for years, but if you take that other offer I can't keep vouching for you" — your mentor ties the request to the support you rely on.
examples.Institutional: The label's renewal talks open with reminders of the relationships the artist would lose — the team, the producer, the radio contacts — if they don't stay on the same terms.
examples.Civilizational: The idea that the industry is one big family means leaving a deal can feel like losing everyone, and that fear does the work of the request.

tactics.name: Intimidation
tactics.definition: Danger is communicated without being stated outright: through words, posture, size, closeness or what is done in front of you.
tactics.also_called: Form Intimidation; Implied Threat; Nonverbal Dominance; Postural Dominance; Spatial Invasion; Threats of Harm; Withdrawal Pressure

examples.Individual: The promoter leans into your space backstage, blocks the corridor to the dressing room and keeps talking about "what you owe the night" while you look for a way past.
examples.Institutional: Negotiation rooms where the artist's side is outnumbered by suits, the head of business affairs never smiles, and silence after each ask is the house style — intimidation as meeting culture.
examples.Civilizational: The image of the cold, unreadable industry boss as a sign of power — so being stared down in a meeting feels like how deals are done rather than pressure.

tactics.name: Concern Trolling / Shame-as-Governance
tactics.definition: Control or criticism is wrapped in the language of worry, so objecting makes you look ungrateful for the care.
tactics.also_called: Concern Masking; Concern Trolling; Shame-as-Governance; Shame-as-Governance Disguised as Advice

examples.Individual: Your mentor says "a real professional wouldn't need to ask about money" — advice that leaves you feeling small for wanting to know your pay.
examples.Institutional: Artist development workshops teach gratitude, humility and "not being a diva" while never explaining contract basics — moralising dressed as guidance.
examples.Civilizational: "Be grateful you're even here" gets passed down as wisdom, and what it teaches is to stay small and quiet.

tactics.name: Ultimatums
tactics.definition: A demand is paired with a loss and a deadline, leaving no room to discuss either.

examples.Individual: "Sign the extension by Monday or you're off the tour, and this isn't a conversation" — the manager pairs a demand with a loss and a deadline, and shuts the door on talking.
examples.Institutional: A distributor sends artists new terms with a short window to accept, and anyone who doesn't sign by the date has their catalogue pulled from release — no room to discuss either part.
examples.Civilizational: "Take it or leave it" is treated as how serious deals are done, so a demand with a loss and a clock attached looks like ordinary business.

tactics.name: Loyalty Binds
tactics.definition: Speaking about a problem is framed as betraying the family, group or cause, so loyalty requires silence.

examples.Individual: "We keep things inside this crew — going to the label would betray everyone who's carried you" — your producer makes silence the price of belonging.
examples.Institutional: A collective's agreement asks members to raise every dispute internally first and frames public complaints as damaging the whole roster — loyalty written in as quiet.
examples.Civilizational: The code of not airing the band's laundry turns speaking about a problem into betraying the family, so loyalty and silence look like the same thing.

tactics.name: Ambient Sexual Threat
tactics.definition: Remarks about your body, sexual jokes and unwanted closeness create a climate in which you feel at risk, without any single act that is easy to report.

examples.Individual: The engineer comments on your outfit, sits too close at the desk and laughs along with the crew's jokes about you — no single moment you could report, but you stop booking late sessions.
examples.Institutional: A studio where suggestive jokes and comments about artists' bodies are part of the "vibe" and complaints are met with "that's just the room" — a climate nobody wrote down but everyone lives in.
examples.Civilizational: The idea that sex is part of the rock-and-roll package makes unwanted closeness and remarks seem like atmosphere, which leaves people feeling at risk without a clear thing to name.

tactics.name: Overcorrection Demands
tactics.definition: After a small mistake, the response demanded, such as apologies, rituals or self-punishment, is far out of scale.

examples.Individual: After your post criticising the label, your manager tells you to record a video apology to the CEO or you'll be dropped, and he stands over you while you record it.
examples.Institutional: Labels that require artists to issue public apologies, retract statements or sign acknowledgments of wrongdoing before any support or release is restored.
examples.Civilizational: The industry habit of demanding public contrition from artists who speak up — which reinforces that the powerful decide when a matter is closed.

tactics.name: Blackmail / Leverage Exploitation
tactics.definition: A demand comes with a threat to expose something about you, or an old secret or debt is kept in reserve as leverage.

examples.Individual: Your old producer mentions, just once, that he "still has those rough demos and the messages from that night" — he never uses them, only lets you know they're there.
examples.Institutional: A label keeps files of an artist's past mistakes and unreleased material and refers to them during renegotiation — a reserve that sits in the background of every conversation.
examples.Civilizational: The tabloid habit of digging up an artist's past teaches everyone in the business that an old secret is a card someone can play, so artists live careful of what others hold.

tactics.name: Moral Outrage as Weapon
tactics.definition: Public outrage is directed at a person in a way that skips any check of what they actually did.

examples.Individual: Someone posts a clip of you cut mid-sentence from a backstage interview, and by morning festival bookers are dropping you — nobody asks what you actually said.
examples.Institutional: A label drops an artist within hours of an online pile-on and issues a statement before reviewing the full footage — outrage acted on without any check of what happened.
examples.Civilizational: The speed of the cancellation cycle means an accusation becomes a verdict before anyone has checked it, and the artist is answering to the outrage, not to the facts.

tactics.name: Emotional Hostage-Taking
tactics.definition: One person's distress rises and falls with your choices, so you end up managing their state instead of making your own decisions.

examples.Individual: Your manager goes silent and sulky for days whenever you take advice from another producer — you start picking collaborators by how he'll react, not by what the song needs.
examples.Institutional: A label head whose mood sets the whole office's week, so artists learn to time requests and choices around keeping him calm rather than what their careers need.
examples.Civilizational: The romance of the tortured genius makes it normal for everyone near a powerful figure to manage that person's feelings, and their own decisions come second.

tactics.name: "I Know Best" Paternalism / Velvet Glove Control
tactics.definition: Another adult decides what is good for you and acts on it, overriding your own choices as being for your own good.
tactics.also_called: "I Know Best" Paternalism; Using Privilege; Velvet Glove Control

examples.Individual: You choose the stripped-back single, and your manager quietly sends the label the remix instead — "trust me, you'll thank me later" overrides the choice you made.
examples.Institutional: Development deals that let the label decide the artist's image, sound and release plan "for their own good," with the artist's preferences treated as inexperience.
examples.Civilizational: The belief that young artists can't know what's best for their own careers lets older industry figures override their choices and call it protection.

tactics.name: Interrogation
tactics.definition: Questions come in a rapid, repeated, accusing stream, so answering feels like a trial rather than a conversation.

examples.Individual: "Who were you with? Why did you post that? Why does that not match what you told me?" — your manager fires questions faster than you can answer, until the van feels like a courtroom.
examples.Institutional: A label's "review meeting" after an artist misses a show puts them in front of several executives taking turns asking the same accusing questions — answering feels like a trial.
examples.Civilizational: "Accountability" in the business can mean being grilled rather than heard, so a barrage of questions passes for professionalism instead of pressure.

tactics.name: Moving-in-Silence
tactics.definition: Something large that will change your life is decided and arranged without you, and you learn about it when it is done.

examples.Individual: You come back from a short break to find your release date moved, your producer reassigned and the tour cancelled — all decided while you were away, and you're the last to know.
examples.Institutional: A label sells an artist's catalogue to another company and the artist finds out from a press release — something that changes their life, arranged without them.
examples.Civilizational: The view that artists don't need to be in the business rooms means big decisions about their work are made around them and announced when they're done.

tactics.name: Enforcing Trivial Demands
tactics.definition: Small rules with no clear purpose are enforced strictly, so obedience itself becomes the point.

examples.Individual: The tour manager makes you redo the whole soundcheck because your water bottle was on the wrong side of the riser — the sound was fine, so the lesson becomes obedience.
examples.Institutional: A development program fines its artists for small slips — a late reply to a group message, the wrong colour on rehearsal days — rules with no clear purpose that make compliance the point.
examples.Civilizational: The belief that discipline is what separates professionals from amateurs makes strict, pointless rules look like training rather than control.

tactics.name: Choice Restriction
tactics.definition: Your realistic options are narrowed through money, access, information or framing until only the wanted choice remains, while you are told the choice is yours.
tactics.also_called: Bounded Choice; Coercive Framing; Institutional Adoption; Reflexive Control; Token Autonomy; Token Autonomy / Coercive Framing

examples.Individual: "You're totally free to choose — the label's version of the single or no single at all" — your manager presents the ultimatum as creative freedom.
examples.Institutional: Contracts that offer artists "approval rights" that can only be used within options the label has already chosen, so control is dressed as choice.
examples.Civilizational: The story that signing is always a free decision — which makes a choice between a bad deal and no career look like opportunity rather than pressure.

tactics.name: Pseudo-Consultation
tactics.definition: A consultation, survey or listening session happens in form, but the decision was already made and does not change.
tactics.also_called: Pre-Decision Concealment; Process Performance; Structural Dilution

examples.Individual: Your manager asks you to "share your thoughts" on the album sequence, nods and thanks you — and the tracklist sent to the label next morning is the one he'd already drafted.
examples.Institutional: A label holds "artist listening sessions" about new contract terms that were finalised weeks before — consultation in form, the decision unchanged.
examples.Civilizational: Being asked for input is treated as being heard, so artists leave a meeting feeling included in a choice that was never open.

tactics.name: Weaponized Inclusion / Strategic Containment
tactics.definition: Critics are invited inside, onto a committee or into a process, where their energy is absorbed and their voice contained.
tactics.also_called: Critique Absorption; Dissent Absorption; Inclusion Capture

examples.Individual: After you raise the missing credits, the label invites you onto its "artist advisory panel" — months of meetings later, your complaint lives in a draft no one has read.
examples.Institutional: A label sets up an "artist council" and gives the loudest critics seats on it, where their concerns are absorbed into slow working groups and never reach the board.
examples.Civilizational: A seat at the table is treated as the reward for speaking up, so being brought inside looks like progress while it quietly contains the voice that spoke.

tactics.name: Controlled Opposition
tactics.definition: Resistance that looks independent is quietly guided or set up by the party it opposes.

examples.Individual: You join the "independent" artists' group pushing back on the label's terms, then learn its organiser runs every statement past the label's lawyers first — the resistance was being steered by the side it opposed.
examples.Institutional: A major funds an artists' rights campaign through a side company, so the campaign's demands never go beyond what the company was ready to give.
examples.Civilizational: Because rebellion sells in the business, the industry is comfortable with protest it has shaped itself, and real opposition gets drowned out by the version it manages.

tactics.name: Manufactured Consent
tactics.definition: Agreement that looks freely given rests on a narrowed picture, on pressure, or on silence counted as a yes.
tactics.also_called: Consent Fabrication; Democratic Validation; Mutual Agreement Fabrication; Silence Harvesting

examples.Individual: Your manager emails the new terms at midnight with "if I don't hear back by morning I'll take that as a yes" — your silence while you sleep is counted as your agreement.
examples.Institutional: A label's standard deal lets it change royalty rates by notice, with continued releases treated as acceptance — agreement that rests on artists not noticing.
examples.Civilizational: "Everyone signs this" makes agreement look freely given when the alternatives were never shown, so a narrowed choice passes for consent.

tactics.name: Sacred Science
tactics.definition: The group's founding ideas are placed beyond evidence or question, so doubting them is treated as a flaw in the doubter.

examples.Individual: When you question the producer's "hit formula," he says "if it didn't chart, you didn't commit to it" — doubting the method becomes a flaw in you.
examples.Institutional: A development program presents its founder's system for building stars as proven beyond question, and trainees who doubt it are marked as "not ready for the process."
examples.Civilizational: The industry's belief in the gut of a few legendary hitmakers puts their rules beyond evidence, so an artist who doubts them looks naive rather than thoughtful.

tactics.name: Doctrine Over Person
tactics.definition: A member's own experience is never allowed to count against the doctrine; when they clash, the person is wrong.

examples.Individual: You tell your vocal coach the method is straining your voice, and she says the method has made stars, so you must be doing it wrong — your own throat can't count against the doctrine.
examples.Institutional: A label's artist-development manual treats every failure as the artist's lack of effort, and an artist's account of what didn't work is filed as an excuse.
examples.Civilizational: "Trust the process" is repeated so often that what an artist actually lives through is never allowed to count against how things are supposed to work.

tactics.name: Forced Confession / Self-Criticism Rituals
tactics.definition: Members must regularly confess faults or criticize themselves before others, and what they say is kept and can be used later.

examples.Individual: Every week in the band meeting your manager has each of you name "what I did wrong this week," and months later he quotes your own words back to you when you ask for a bigger split.
examples.Institutional: A development program runs group "honesty sessions" where trainees confess their failings in front of staff, and the notes go into files later used in contract reviews.
examples.Civilizational: The belief that real artists must be ruthlessly self-critical makes confessing faults in public look like growth, and what is said stays on record.

tactics.name: Algorithmic Manipulation
tactics.definition: Feeds and recommendation lists decide what you see first and most often, steering attention and mood in ways you cannot see.

examples.Individual: The platform's artist dashboard always opens on the paid promotion it wants you to buy and buries your organic numbers — you think you're checking your stats, but your attention is being steered.
examples.Institutional: A streaming service's recommendation lists push the label's priority tracks to the top of every listener's queue, so what fans hear first is decided by systems they cannot see.
examples.Civilizational: The belief that the feed simply shows what people like hides how much it shapes what they hear, and artists end up chasing an audience the system has already sorted.

tactics.name: Biometric Exploitation
tactics.definition: Signals of how you feel, read from your face, voice or body by cameras, microphones and wearables, are used to influence you.

examples.Individual: At the audition the casting producer films your face close-up as you hear the panel's notes, and later the show cuts your reaction to make you look broken — your feelings read off your face and used.
examples.Institutional: A live-event app reads fans' heart rates from wearables during the show and pushes merch offers at the peak moments — signals from the body turned into sales pressure.
examples.Civilizational: The idea that tracking reactions is just better audience research makes reading people's faces and bodies feel normal, even when it is used to move them.

tactics.name: Institutional Capture
tactics.definition: Influence is gained over the bodies meant to provide oversight, or outside structures are lined up to enforce, so the place you would turn to for help is already on their side.

examples.Individual: Your ex-manager tells promoters you're "unreliable" and the booking agent stops answering your calls — people outside the deal now carry out his decision.
examples.Institutional: Labels that use relationships with promoters, playlist editors, press and venues to ensure an artist who left can't get bookings, coverage or support.
examples.Civilizational: The idea that the industry is one big network that always protects its own — which turns outside players into enforcers of whoever holds the most power.

tactics.name: Arbitrary Authority
tactics.definition: Decisions follow no stated rule, so nothing you do reliably changes the outcome.

examples.Individual: The same kind of demo gets a "this is the one" from the A&R one month and "not even close" the next, with no reason either time — you stop believing anything you do changes the outcome.
examples.Institutional: A label decides which artists get a release slot with no stated criteria, and the same results earn a push for one artist and a shelf for another.
examples.Civilizational: "Nobody knows anything in this business" makes random decisions feel like fate, so artists stop expecting their work to be what counts.

tactics.name: Black-Box Decisions
tactics.definition: Consequential decisions come from a system whose workings cannot be seen, explained or meaningfully questioned.
tactics.also_called: High-Stakes Consequence; Invisibility of the Mechanism

examples.Individual: Your track is suddenly pulled from the platform for "suspicious activity," and when you ask why, the distributor says nobody there can see how the system decided.
examples.Institutional: A streaming service's payout and playlist decisions come from systems no one at the label or the artist's team can explain or appeal in any meaningful way.
examples.Civilizational: The belief that the algorithm is neutral and too complex to question means decisions that shape whole careers are accepted without anyone being able to look inside.

tactics.name: Celebration as Cover
tactics.definition: Overwork, self-funding or sacrifice is praised in public as dedication, so the shortage that required it is never fixed.
tactics.also_called: Celebration Capture; Celebration as Extraction Cover

examples.Individual: At the end of tour your manager toasts you for paying the crew out of your own fee and playing through illness — the applause makes the shortfall sound like your dedication.
examples.Institutional: A label's awards night honours the artist who "made the album on their own dime" — praise that keeps the missing budget from ever being fixed.
examples.Civilizational: The legend of the starving artist turns self-funding and burnout into proof of commitment, so the gaps that caused them are celebrated instead of closed.

tactics.name: Closed-Loop Appeals
tactics.definition: Challenging a decision sends you back to the same people, rules or system that made it.

examples.Individual: You dispute your royalty statement, and the dispute goes back to the same accountant who produced it — who confirms it and notes the process was followed.
examples.Institutional: A label's contract sends every artist grievance to an internal review run by the business affairs team that wrote the terms — an appeal that loops back to its source.
examples.Civilizational: "Take it up with the label" sounds like a route to fairness, but in the business it usually means asking the people who made the decision to judge it.

tactics.name: Collective Punishment
tactics.definition: A whole group is punished for something one person did, or for something no one is named for, so the group turns its pressure inward.
tactics.also_called: Collective Consequence; Incident Identification Without Individual Accountability

examples.Individual: Someone leaks a track from the session, and the producer cancels everyone's credits on the album until "somebody owns up" — the other writers start leaning on the newest one to confess.
examples.Institutional: After one artist's public complaint, the label freezes marketing for the whole roster "until things settle" — and artists start pressuring each other to stay quiet.
examples.Civilizational: The idea that one artist's trouble reflects on the whole scene lets punishment fall on everyone, which turns the group against whoever might speak.

tactics.name: Data Harvesting
tactics.definition: Detailed information about behavior, location, feelings or performance is collected continuously and built into a profile, far beyond what the service needs.
tactics.also_called: Ambient Data Collection; Data Accumulation; Data Point Extraction; Profile Construction

examples.Individual: The fan app your label made you promote logs where every listener is, what they play at night and who they share with — far more than you need to sell a ticket.
examples.Institutional: A label's artist portal tracks its own artists' sleep, location and social activity through linked devices and accounts, building a profile far beyond what the work requires.
examples.Civilizational: "Data is how you know your fans" makes constant collection feel like good marketing, so a detailed record of people's lives is gathered as a matter of routine.

tactics.name: Data Onward Sharing
tactics.definition: Information collected for one purpose is passed, sold or shown to others, often described as anonymized, without the person's real knowledge.
tactics.also_called: De-identification Laundering; Non-Consensual Distribution; Secondary Market Exploitation

examples.Individual: You fill in the label's "wellbeing check-in" before the tour, and soon after the promoter seems to know you've been struggling — what you shared for one reason travelled.
examples.Institutional: A ticketing company passes fan purchase and location records to sponsors and brand partners, described as anonymised, without fans really knowing who sees them.
examples.Civilizational: The assumption that any information collected in the business can be used for marketing lets data move from one use to another without anyone asking.

tactics.name: Development Subordination
tactics.definition: A person's own learning, health or future is ranked below their usefulness to the system, and that ranking is presented as opportunity.

examples.Individual: Your producer keeps you writing toplines for his other artists instead of finishing your own record, calling it "a great opportunity" — your career slows while your usefulness grows.
examples.Institutional: A development deal books its young artists as backing singers and openers for the label's priority acts for years, presented as experience while their own releases wait.
examples.Civilizational: "Pay your dues" ranks an artist's own growth and health below what they can do for others, and makes that ranking sound like a chance.

tactics.name: Initiative Churn
tactics.definition: New programs are launched one after another, so activity looks like progress while none runs long enough to be judged.

examples.Individual: Every few months your manager announces a new plan — a new image, a new producer, a new content schedule — and you never stay with one long enough to know if any of it helped.
examples.Institutional: A label rolls out a new artist-development program each year, with new names and new staff, so activity looks like progress while none runs long enough to be judged.
examples.Civilizational: The business's appetite for the next big thing makes constant reinvention look like strategy, and no one stays still long enough to ask what worked.

tactics.name: Labor Extraction
tactics.definition: Work, time, care or personal money beyond what was agreed or paid is expected and uncounted, often because the role has grown too big or because stopping would hurt the people you serve.
tactics.also_called: Administrative Displacement; Compassion Exploitation; Invisibility of Clinical Labor; Performance Extraction; Personal Subsidy Extraction; Ratio Exploitation; Role Inflation; Role Overload

examples.Individual: Your manager expects you to run the socials, sell merch after every show and drive the van overnight — none of it in your deal, all of it "just what artists do now."
examples.Institutional: A label's standard contract leaves content creation, fan engagement and promo travel uncounted, so artists pay with their own time and money for work the company used to fund.
examples.Civilizational: "Do it for the love" makes unpaid hours and personal spending look like passion, so the extra work is never counted or paid.

tactics.name: Liability Reframing
tactics.definition: A duty to protect or repair is handed to legal or risk management and treated as exposure to limit, then declared expired, out of scope or not owed.

examples.Individual: You report that a crew member assaulted a dancer on tour, and instead of the tour manager you're put on a call with the label's lawyers, who say it happened "off the clock and outside our scope."
examples.Institutional: A production company sends every safety complaint straight to risk management, which assesses exposure and then declares the claim out of time or not the company's duty.
examples.Civilizational: The habit of treating harm on the road as a legal risk rather than a duty of care lets the business close matters on paper that were never repaired.

tactics.name: Metric-Mission Substitution
tactics.definition: The numbers chosen to measure a purpose quietly replace the purpose, and people are judged on the numbers.
tactics.also_called: Engagement-Learning Conflation; Metric Installation; Metric Substitution

examples.Individual: Your A&R stops talking about the songs and only asks about saves and skip rates — "this is what we're judged on" — and the numbers take the place of the music.
examples.Institutional: A label sets artists' budgets by streaming targets alone, so tracks are cut and shaped to hit the metric rather than to say anything.
examples.Civilizational: "The numbers don't lie" lets chart and stream counts stand in for what music is for, and artists get judged on the count.

tactics.name: Motivation Displacement
tactics.definition: Points, scores and rewards replace a person's own reasons for doing something, so they stop when the reward stops.
tactics.also_called: Intrinsic Motivation Displacement; Intrinsic-Extrinsic Displacement; Joy Extinction

examples.Individual: You used to write every day for the joy of it until your manager started paying bonuses per viral clip — now you write for clips, and when the bonuses stop, so does the writing.
examples.Institutional: A platform's creator program pays and ranks artists by points for posting, so they post for the points and drop off when the payments end.
examples.Civilizational: The constant language of streams, followers and badges replaces the reasons people started making music, so the drive fades once the rewards do.

tactics.name: Predictive Tracking
tactics.definition: People are routed into tracks, groups or labels on the strength of a prediction, and the track then limits what they are offered and can become.
tactics.also_called: Automatic Sorting; Intervention Channeling; Track Solidification

examples.Individual: After your first single underperforms, the label marks you as a "developing" act, and years later the A&R says bigger budgets "aren't on your track" — the prediction became your ceiling.
examples.Institutional: A distributor sorts new artists into tiers by early data, and the tier then decides what promotion, playlists and support they are ever offered.
examples.Civilizational: The belief that you can tell who will make it from the first numbers means early guesses decide careers, and the guess comes true because of how people are treated.

tactics.name: Strategic Delay
tactics.definition: Responses, records or decisions are slowed until deadlines pass, evidence fades or the person gives up.
tactics.also_called: Access Delay; Recommendation Deferral; Timeline Elongation; Timeline Exploitation

examples.Individual: You ask your old label for your royalty records before the rights deadline, and they say "next week" every time — until the window to reclaim your masters has closed.
examples.Institutional: A label answers audit requests with slow back-and-forth over paperwork until the contract's time limit for disputes runs out.
examples.Civilizational: "These things take time in this business" makes long delays look normal, so waiting out the person who asked becomes an ordinary way to end a dispute.

tactics.name: Strategic Timing
tactics.definition: Damaging information or sudden pressure arrives just before an important moment, leaving no time to check or respond.

examples.Individual: The night before your showcase, your manager tells you the label has "serious doubts" about your new songs — no time to ask what they mean before you walk on stage.
examples.Institutional: A label sends an artist a breach notice the day before an album launch, so the artist has to choose between the launch and answering it properly.
examples.Civilizational: The rush around releases and tours means bad news arriving at the worst moment is treated as bad luck, and nobody asks why it always lands then.

tactics.name: Structural Underfunding
tactics.definition: The service meant to help is kept too small, too thinly staffed or too run-down to work, and its failure is treated as nobody's fault.

examples.Individual: You wait weeks to see the label's one artist-care officer, who covers the whole roster — and when you get in, she apologises: "it's just how it is here."
examples.Institutional: A label advertises mental-health support for its artists but funds it so thinly that most requests go unanswered, and the gaps are treated as nobody's fault.
examples.Civilizational: The view that support for artists is a luxury the business can't afford keeps the help small and lets its failure pass as the way things are.

tactics.name: Harm to Pets or Property
tactics.definition: Belongings are destroyed, or a pet is harmed or threatened, as a warning of what could happen next. (Treat as a safety risk: contact local emergency or domestic violence services.)

examples.Individual: After you argue about leaving the band, your manager smashes the guitar you write every song on — nothing is said about you, but the message is clear. This is a safety risk; local emergency or domestic violence services can help.
examples.Institutional: A tour where an artist's gear keeps getting "accidentally" damaged after disputes with a powerful figure, and staff treat it as wear and tear — a warning that the company never names. Such patterns belong with safety services, not with the person doing it.
examples.Civilizational: The rock-and-roll image of smashed rooms and broken gear makes destruction look like part of the culture, which can hide when it is being used as a warning against someone.

tactics.name: Coerced Debt
tactics.definition: Loans, credit or bills are taken out in your name, or you are pressured into them, without real consent, so you carry debt for someone else's control.

examples.Individual: Your manager uses your details to take out loans for "tour costs" in your name, and the debt letters arrive at your address — debt you never really agreed to carry.
examples.Institutional: A management company has young artists sign personal guarantees for equipment and studio credit as a condition of the deal, so the artist carries debt for decisions the company makes.
examples.Civilizational: The belief that artists must invest in themselves at any cost makes debt in their own name look normal, even when someone else controls the spending.

tactics.name: Debt Bondage
tactics.definition: Fees for travel, housing, training or recruitment are charged against future earnings and keep growing, so you must keep working to pay a debt that never clears.

examples.Individual: The agency that brought you over for the residency deducts "housing, flights and training" from every fee — after months of shows you owe more than when you arrived.
examples.Institutional: Development deals that charge trainees for lessons, lodging and styling against future earnings, with the balance growing faster than any income can clear it.
examples.Civilizational: "Everything is recoupable" makes a debt that never clears look like standard industry accounting, so artists keep working to pay off their own start.

tactics.name: Document Confiscation
tactics.definition: Passports, identity papers, visas or certificates are taken "for safekeeping", so leaving, travelling or proving who you are depends on someone else.

examples.Individual: The tour promoter keeps your passport "for the border crossings" — every time you ask for it back, there's a reason to wait. Independent support services can help with getting documents returned.
examples.Institutional: Overseas performance agencies that hold performers' passports and visas "for safekeeping" for the length of the contract, so leaving depends on the agency.
examples.Civilizational: The idea that the tour handles all the paperwork makes it seem normal for someone else to hold your papers, and with them your ability to leave.

tactics.name: Status Threats
tactics.definition: Your visa, residency, enrollment or legal status is used as a threat: comply, or you or your family could be reported, removed or deported. (Route to independent legal advice and support services.)

examples.Individual: "Complain about the pay and I'll tell immigration your work visa isn't in order," the club owner says — your right to stay becomes the leverage. Independent legal advice can tell you where you actually stand.
examples.Institutional: Agencies that sponsor foreign performers and hint that complaints will end the sponsorship — status used to keep people quiet. Independent legal advice and support services can help.
examples.Civilizational: The assumption that touring performers from abroad should be grateful for the chance lets threats about status pass as the cost of the dream.

tactics.name: Enmeshment
tactics.definition: The line between two people's feelings, choices and identities is dissolved, so your moods, decisions and successes are treated as belonging to someone else. (A family-systems concept.)

examples.Individual: Your father, who manages you, says "we've got a number one" and sulks for days when you mention working with someone else — your career is treated as his life.
examples.Institutional: Family-run management setups where a parent's identity, income and moods are tied to the artist's success, so the artist's choices are treated as belonging to the family.
examples.Civilizational: The story of the stage parent who lives through the child's success makes this blending of lives look like devotion rather than something that takes the artist's self away.

tactics.name: Apologies Without Repair
tactics.definition: Performed remorse with no change.

examples.Individual: "I'm sorry, I was stressed, it won't happen again" — your manager says it after every blow-up, and the next week the shouting starts again.
examples.Institutional: "We take these concerns seriously and are reviewing our practices" — the label's statement after a scandal, followed by no policy change, no repayment and the same executive in charge.
examples.Civilizational: The industry cycle of public apologies after each exposure — which teaches audiences to accept regret as resolution while the conditions that caused the harm stay in place.

tactics.name: Pity Plays
tactics.definition: Performing victimhood to prevent accountability.
tactics.also_called: Strategic Self-Deprecation; Strategic Self-Deprecation / Performed Humility; Strategic Vulnerability; Strategic Vulnerability / Weaponized Tears; Weaponized Tears

examples.Individual: When you confront the producer about your missing credit, he tells you how hard his year has been, how broke he is, how everyone uses him — and you end up comforting him.
examples.Institutional: Executives who respond to allegations with emotional public statements about their own pain and mental health, shifting the focus away from what they're accused of.
examples.Civilizational: The cultural reflex to rally around whoever cries most visibly — which can turn emotion into a shield and leave the original complaint unheard.

tactics.name: Forced Forgiveness / Weaponized Forgiveness
tactics.definition: "Move on" before harm is processed.

examples.Individual: "It's in the past, we've got a tour to do — can we just move on?" — the band leader pushes you to drop the incident before you've had time to understand it.
examples.Institutional: Settlement agreements and HR processes that close complaints quickly with a payment and an NDA, ending the matter before the person harmed has recovered.
examples.Civilizational: The cultural pressure to "be the bigger person" — which treats instant forgiveness as maturity and leaves harm unprocessed and repeatable.

tactics.name: Competitive Victimhood
tactics.definition: Responding to your pain with their bigger pain.

examples.Individual: You tell your bandmate you were humiliated on stage, and he says "you think that's bad? Do you know what I went through on my first tour?" — your hurt gets swallowed by his story.
examples.Institutional: Label cultures where senior artists and executives respond to complaints from newcomers with tales of their own early suffering, setting a bar no one is allowed to complain under.
examples.Civilizational: "You have to pay your dues" — the cultural script that turns every story of harm into a contest, so the newest pain always counts for less.

tactics.name: Aftercare Control
tactics.definition: "That was for your good" reframing harm as help.

examples.Individual: "I pushed you that hard in the studio because I knew you could take it — that's why your voice is so good now" — the producer recasts months of harsh treatment as a gift.
examples.Institutional: Development programs that describe gruelling schedules, public criticism and isolation as "artist training," framing harm as the price of growth.
examples.Civilizational: The belief that tough treatment builds great artists — which makes it hard to name harm because the industry calls it mentorship.

tactics.name: Legal Abuse
tactics.definition: Lawsuits, court filings and legal processes are used to drain, punish or silence someone, for example after they leave or speak out. (Route to qualified legal advice.)

examples.Individual: After you leave, your old manager sues for commission on every future song you write, and the court dates keep coming — your new career stuck in legal limbo.
examples.Institutional: Labels that respond to an artist's exit by filing claims, injunction requests and audit challenges, knowing the process alone will drain the artist's time and money.
examples.Civilizational: The belief that the big side always wins in court — which turns the threat of endless litigation into a way to punish those who walk away.

tactics.name: Humiliation Rituals
tactics.definition: Degradation disguised as development.

examples.Individual: At rehearsal, the choreographer makes you repeat the move alone while the whole crew watches and laughs — "it's how we toughen up new dancers."
examples.Institutional: Talent shows and development camps that build humiliation into the format — public critiques, elimination ceremonies, harsh mock auditions — framed as preparation for the real industry.
examples.Civilizational: The belief that humiliation is part of becoming a professional — which makes degrading treatment feel like a rite of passage rather than harm.

tactics.name: Public Exposure
tactics.definition: Being singled out for shaming.
tactics.also_called: Public Humiliation; Public Identification; Public Shaming

examples.Individual: Your manager reads out your bad streaming numbers in front of the whole team, saying "this is what happens when you don't listen."
examples.Institutional: Label meetings where underperforming artists are singled out in front of others, using the comparison to put pressure on everyone in the room.
examples.Civilizational: The culture of public "call-outs" in the industry — which teaches artists that being shamed in front of others is how accountability works.

tactics.name: Ghosting as Control
tactics.definition: Disappearing without closure.

examples.Individual: The A&R rep who called you every day for months suddenly stops answering — no email, no explanation, just silence after the deal falls through.
examples.Institutional: Labels and agencies that drop artists by simply ceasing contact — no termination letter, no explanation, just no more calls or releases.
examples.Civilizational: The cultural acceptance of silent exits in the industry — which leaves people unsure what happened and makes them blame themselves.

tactics.name: Sudden Devaluation
tactics.definition: An abrupt shift from investment to disposal.

examples.Individual: One week your manager says you're his priority, the next he says the label is moving on and he's taking on a new artist — the switch happens overnight.
examples.Institutional: Labels that drop marketing, cancel releases and stop calling an artist almost immediately after a single underperforms.
examples.Civilizational: The industry's love of hype and impatience — which makes sudden abandonment look normal and teaches artists to expect it.

tactics.name: Replacement Display
tactics.definition: Publicly showcasing your replacement to signal your disposability.

examples.Individual: Your old producer posts photos in the studio with a younger singer, captioned "the new voice of the project," a week after dropping you.
examples.Institutional: Labels that announce new signings with fanfare right after an artist leaves, using the publicity to signal that the departed artist was easily replaced.
examples.Civilizational: The industry's constant "next big thing" narrative — which makes every artist feel replaceable and keeps them anxious about holding their place.

tactics.name: Blame Discard
tactics.definition: Framing the discard as the target's fault.

examples.Individual: "We had to let you go because you were too difficult to work with" — the label says it after you asked for an audit, framing the drop as your fault.
examples.Institutional: Companies that justify dropping artists by citing "bad attitude," "lack of commitment" or "creative differences," so the artist carries the blame for the end of the deal.
examples.Civilizational: The belief that if you're dropped, you must have done something wrong — which puts responsibility for the system's choices on the artist.

tactics.name: Managed Exit
tactics.definition: Orchestrating the departure to maximize the system's control over the narrative.

examples.Individual: "We'll put out a statement saying it was mutual, and you'll sign this agreement not to talk about it" — your exit is managed so that only the label's version exists.
examples.Institutional: Labels that organize departures with joint statements, NDAs and controlled press releases, so the public never hears the artist's account.
examples.Civilizational: The industry habit of tidy, "mutual" separations — which hides real stories and keeps power with those who wrote the exit.

tactics.name: Manufactured Closure
tactics.definition: The matter is declared resolved or closed by the side that caused it, without the harmed person agreeing and without the harm being named.
tactics.also_called: Closure Manufacture; Quiet Resolution; Resolution Without Acknowledgment; Unilateral Resolution

examples.Individual: After months of complaints about the producer, you get an email from the label saying "we consider this matter closed" — nobody asked if you agreed, and nothing says what happened.
examples.Institutional: A label announces it has "resolved" an artist's dispute in a press statement the artist never saw, naming no harm and offering no change.
examples.Civilizational: The rush to "move on" in the business lets the side that caused harm declare it over, and the harmed person is expected to treat the statement as the end.

tactics.name: Paid Silence
tactics.definition: Money, a reference, a role or another benefit is offered in exchange for not speaking about what happened.

examples.Individual: After you report the tour manager, your manager offers you the opening slot on the big tour "as long as this stays between us" — the slot is the price of your silence.
examples.Institutional: Settlements that come with release bonuses or new album budgets attached to strict confidentiality clauses — benefit offered on the condition that the artist never speaks about what happened.
examples.Civilizational: The industry's habit of making problems "go away quietly" turns money and opportunity into the normal answer to harm, and silence into part of the deal.

tactics.name: Punitive Transfer
tactics.definition: After raising a concern, the person is moved to a different place, team, class or role, presented as routine.

examples.Individual: The week after you complain about the producer, the label moves you to a different studio and team "to freshen up your sound" — routine on paper, and you, not him, are the one moved.
examples.Institutional: A label shifts artists who raise concerns to a smaller imprint or a later release cycle, described as a normal roster change.
examples.Civilizational: "Shake-ups happen all the time" makes a move after a complaint look like ordinary business, so the person who spoke up absorbs the disruption.

tactics.name: Record Erasure
tactics.definition: Records, files or evidence of what happened are deleted, lost or sealed, so the event can later be denied.

examples.Individual: The messages you sent the tour manager about the incident are gone from the shared tour chat when you look for them later — without them, the company can say nothing was reported.
examples.Institutional: A label's settlement includes the deletion of internal emails and complaint files about the matter, so the event can later be denied with nothing on record.
examples.Civilizational: The belief that old trouble is best left buried makes lost files and wiped records seem tidy, and history can then be told without what happened.

tactics.name: Uncorrected Record
tactics.definition: The accusation is public, loud and lasting, while any correction is quiet or missing, so the first version stays.

examples.Individual: The producer tells a packed studio you stole his beat, and when the credits are quietly fixed weeks later, no one tells the room — they still remember the accusation.
examples.Institutional: A label's public statement accusing an artist of breaching contract runs everywhere, while the later correction goes out as a single line on a page nobody visits.
examples.Civilizational: Headlines about artists travel far faster than retractions, so the first version of a story tends to be the one the business remembers.

tactics.name: Values-Fit Pretext
tactics.definition: A person's results or questions are redescribed as a mismatch with the group's values or culture, which becomes the reason they have to go.

examples.Individual: After you question the label's spending on your tour, the A&R says you're "just not a fit with our family culture" — your questions become the reason you're dropped.
examples.Institutional: Management companies that end deals with artists who ask about money by citing "misalignment with our values," so the questions never have to be answered.
examples.Civilizational: The language of "vibe" and "chemistry" in the business lets asking hard questions be recast as not fitting in, and fitting in becomes the reason to go.

tactics.name: Visible Impunity
tactics.definition: The person reported faces no visible consequence, which tells everyone watching that reporting does not work.

examples.Individual: You report the tour manager who grabbed a dancer, and next season he's running the same tour with a promotion — everyone who watched learns that reporting does nothing.
examples.Institutional: A label keeps a producer at the top of its roster after repeated complaints, with no public consequence, so everyone working with him learns to stay quiet.
examples.Civilizational: Stories of powerful figures who were reported and never touched become part of the folklore, which tells newcomers that speaking up only costs the speaker.

tactics.name: Swatting
tactics.definition: A false emergency report brings an armed or emergency response to someone's home or school, using the authorities as a weapon. (Treat as an emergency safety risk.)

examples.Individual: After a falling-out with an online fan group, police arrive at your house because someone falsely reported an emergency there. This is an emergency safety risk: follow the officers' instructions and contact emergency services and support afterwards.
examples.Institutional: Artists who stream from home face false emergency calls after online feuds, and platforms treat each case as a one-off — the response is left to the police and the artist alone. Treat any such pattern as an emergency safety matter.
examples.Civilizational: The idea that online feuds are just entertainment can hide how quickly they turn into using emergency services as a weapon against someone's home.

tactics.name: Orbiting
tactics.definition: Watching from a distance to maintain psychological presence after discard.

examples.Individual: Your former producer never messages you, but likes every post, watches every story and shows up at the edge of your shows — always just within sight.
examples.Institutional: Labels that follow a departed artist's career from the sidelines, appearing at industry events or sending representatives to watch without speaking.
examples.Civilizational: The industry habit of "staying friendly" with everyone you've worked with — which makes a former boss watching from the sidelines look like courtesy instead of presence.

tactics.name: Infantilization
tactics.definition: Treating competent people as incapable to maintain dependence.

examples.Individual: "Don't worry your head about contracts, sweetheart, the grown-ups will handle it" — the manager talks to you, an adult with a career, like a child who can't be trusted with paperwork.
examples.Institutional: Labels that keep artists away from business meetings, lawyers and statements, describing them as "creatives" who need protecting from the details of their own careers.
examples.Civilizational: The cultural image of artists as childlike and impractical — which justifies keeping capable adults dependent on the people who handle their money.

tactics.name: Parentification
tactics.definition: Forcing someone into a caretaker role that reverses the natural hierarchy.

examples.Individual: You're the youngest in the band, but you end up keeping the lead singer sober, waking him for shows and calming the label when he disappears — the caretaker for the person meant to lead.
examples.Institutional: Tours where junior crew, assistants or child performers carry the emotional and practical load for unstable senior figures, a role reversal treated as part of the job.
examples.Civilizational: The industry story of the loyal sidekick who holds the star together — which makes being the caretaker of someone with more power look like devotion instead of a reversed hierarchy.

tactics.name: Emotional Blackmail via Self-Harm Threats
tactics.definition: Threatening collapse to prevent departure or boundaries.

examples.Individual: "If you leave this project, I don't know what I'll do to myself" — your collaborator says it when you try to step away, and you stay out of fear. A threat like this is a crisis for professionals and emergency services, not something to carry alone.
examples.Institutional: Teams that keep a struggling artist's partners, crew and family on edge with warnings that any departure could trigger a collapse, so nobody feels free to set limits.
examples.Civilizational: The myth of the fragile genius who must be protected at any cost — which turns threats of collapse into a reason for everyone else to give up their boundaries.

tactics.name: Health Sabotage
tactics.definition: Interfering with wellbeing to maintain dependence or instability.

examples.Individual: Your manager keeps "forgetting" to book the vocal rest days your doctor ordered and schedules extra shows instead — your health quietly worn down while you depend on him.
examples.Institutional: Tours where rest, food, quiet rooms and support for artists in recovery are treated as luxuries, while late nights and pressure on the road are built into the schedule.
examples.Civilizational: The rock-and-roll legend of excess as part of the job — which makes damage to performers' health look like culture instead of something the system allows.

tactics.name: Coordinated Reporting
tactics.definition: Attempting to remove your voice.

examples.Individual: Your videos start getting taken down one after another for "violations," and you notice it began the day after you criticised your old manager online.
examples.Institutional: Rights holders and fan groups that file mass copyright claims or abuse reports against an artist's uploads, using platform rules to pull their voice offline.
examples.Civilizational: The trust that platform takedowns mean someone did something wrong — which lets coordinated reporting silence people under the look of neutral rules.

tactics.name: Context Collapse
tactics.definition: Communications stripped of context to change meaning.
tactics.also_called: Context Collapse Exploitation; Context Elimination; Context Stripping; Evidence Traps; Moment Extraction

examples.Individual: The producer screenshots the one angry text you sent after weeks of being ignored and shows it to the label, leaving out everything that led up to it.
examples.Institutional: Business affairs teams that pull selected emails and messages into a dispute file, cutting away earlier promises and the context that would explain the artist's reaction.
examples.Civilizational: The belief that "the receipts don't lie" — which makes a cropped screenshot feel like proof, even when the missing context changes the meaning completely.

tactics.name: Doxxing
tactics.definition: Publishing private information to intimidate.

examples.Individual: After your public split with the label, your home address and family's names appear in a fan forum, posted by an account linked to your old team. If you feel unsafe, contact the police or a safety service rather than responding.
examples.Institutional: Industry disputes where private details of crew, artists or whistle-blowers leak from contracts, riders and tour documents into public spaces, making speaking up feel physically dangerous.
examples.Civilizational: The belief that public figures give up all privacy — which makes exposing an artist's private life seem like part of fame rather than intimidation.

tactics.name: Forged Screenshots / Edited Evidence
tactics.definition: Fabricated or altered evidence presented as proof.
tactics.also_called: Deepfake Video/Audio; Deepfakes; Edited Recordings; Fabricated Evidence; Forged Screenshots

examples.Individual: Your ex-bandmate posts a screenshot of a message you never sent, saying you threatened him — and people share it before you can show your real chat history.
examples.Institutional: Disputes where edited emails, altered split sheets or doctored session logs are presented as proof of who wrote what, putting the burden on the artist to disprove them.
examples.Civilizational: The belief that a screenshot is evidence — which makes fabricated material persuasive and leaves the person targeted scrambling to prove a negative.

tactics.name: Guilt Legacy
tactics.definition: Inherited obligation used across generations.

examples.Individual: "Your father played in this band and so did his father — walking away would shame the family" — the pressure to stay is passed down like an heirloom.
examples.Institutional: Family-run labels, bands and estates that expect each generation to carry the debts, contracts and loyalties of the last, binding heirs to deals they never chose.
examples.Civilizational: The industry romance of musical dynasties — which makes inherited obligation look like legacy and makes leaving feel like betraying everyone who came before.

tactics.name: Maternal Gatekeeping
tactics.definition: Positioning oneself as the authority over your development to undermine confidence.

examples.Individual: Your parent-manager tells every producer "I know what's best for my child's voice" and overrules your choices in the studio, until you stop trusting your own ear.
examples.Institutional: Child-performer setups where a parent is signatory, manager and financial gatekeeper, so the young artist's growth and decisions all pass through one person. Concerns about a child's welfare belong with child-protection services or a trusted professional.
examples.Civilizational: The cultural belief that a devoted parent always knows best for a young performer — which makes undermining their confidence look like protection.

tactics.name: Smart-Home Coercion
tactics.definition: Connected home devices such as cameras, locks, thermostats and speakers are used to monitor, unsettle or control someone living there.

examples.Individual: Your manager installed the cameras and smart locks in the band house, and now he comments on who visited and changes the door codes when you're "slacking" — home becomes a place you're watched and controlled.
examples.Institutional: Development houses fitted with connected cameras, speakers and locks that staff control remotely, presented as security while they monitor and unsettle the artists living there.
examples.Civilizational: The idea that being watched is just part of fame makes cameras and connected devices in an artist's home seem normal, even when they are used to control the people inside.

tactics.name: AI Voice Cloning
tactics.definition: Software produces speech that sounds like a specific real person, used to deceive the people who know that voice.

examples.Individual: Your bassist gets a voice note in your voice asking him to send the tour money to a new account — the voice was generated, and he trusted it because he knew it.
examples.Institutional: Fake releases built from generated versions of an artist's voice are uploaded under the artist's name, so fans and partners are fooled by a sound they recognise.
examples.Civilizational: Because the business already treats a singer's voice as a product that can be copied and sampled, a cloned voice can pass as the real person before anyone checks.

tactics.name: Intimate Image Abuse
tactics.definition: Real or fabricated intimate images of a person are shared, threatened or used against them without consent. (Treat as an emergency: tell a trusted adult and contact the platform and police or specialist services.)
tactics.also_called: Deepfake / AI Voice / SIM Swap / Intimate Image Abuse / Smart-Home Coercion

examples.Individual: A clip of your voice singing lines you never recorded appears online, then private images surface after a dispute with someone on your old team — your identity turned into a weapon. Image abuse belongs with the platform's reporting tools, a legal adviser and, where you feel unsafe, the police.
